title: Office Entry Sidewalk & Patio Pressure Washing Pricing: Small Suites vs. Large Floors
seoTitle: Small vs Large Office Walkway Pressure Washing: Volume Pricing Compared
metaDescription: Small vs large office walkway pressure washing: 400 sq ft entries pay up to $0.80/sq ft while 15,000 sq ft plazas pay $0.12–$0.22. Compare your volume tier.
excerpt: The square-foot price for washing office entries, sidewalks, and patios falls sharply as the area grows because mobilization is fixed and production speeds up on open plazas. This guide compares small suites, mid-size buildings, and large campuses with real budget math.
quickAnswer: A small office with a 400–800 sq ft entry usually pays the $175–$350 visit minimum, which works out to $0.40–$0.80 per sq ft. Mid-size buildings with 2,000–5,000 sq ft of walkways typically pay $0.18–$0.35 per sq ft, and 25,000+ sq ft buildings with 10,000–20,000 sq ft of plazas and patios often negotiate $0.12–$0.22 per sq ft.

blocks.text: Why small sites pay more per square foot

Pressure washing has a heavy fixed cost per visit. Before a technician cleans a single square foot, the vendor has paid for drive time, loading a trailer-mounted hot-water unit, setting up hoses and cones, covering storm drains, and breaking down at the end. That overhead is roughly 60–90 minutes of crew time plus fuel, which is why minimums sit at $175–$350. A 2,000 sq ft office suite in a strip center might have only a 500 sq ft storefront walk, so the minimum dominates. A 40,000 sq ft headquarters with a 12,000 sq ft entry plaza spreads the same setup across 24 times more surface.

The same economy shows up in interior janitorial pricing. The national benchmarks drop from $0.12–$0.20 per sq ft for offices under 2,500 sq ft to $0.05–$0.10 for 25,000+ sq ft buildings. Exterior washing follows the same curve, only steeper, because the equipment is heavier and the setup longer.

blocks.caption: Effective pressure washing rates by building size and exterior surface area

blocks.text: Production speed improves on large open surfaces

Large plazas let a crew run a 20- or 24-inch rotary surface cleaner in long, straight passes with few edges. Production can climb past 1,500 sq ft per technician hour. Small sites are the opposite: narrow walks, planters, bike racks, benches, curbs, and ADA ramps force wand edging, which can cut production to 500 sq ft per hour. So the small site pays twice: once in minimum charges and again in slower edge work.

The equipment mix shifts with size, too. Covered vestibules and polished concrete thresholds in small buildings are sometimes better served by a twin-brush 12-inch scrub-and-polish machine or a compact cordless scrubber-drier with 1-gallon tanks, which avoids overspray on glass storefronts. Large sites may use a 20-inch 175 RPM rotary floor machine with a scrub brush on covered loggias, and save pressure washing for open-air concrete.

blocks.title: Side-by-side example
blocks.text: A 2,000 sq ft medical-office suite with a 450 sq ft entry walk pays a $250 minimum, which is $0.56 per sq ft. A 30,000 sq ft office building with 9,500 sq ft of walkways and patio, priced at $0.18 per sq ft, pays $1,710, which is 6.8 times the cost for 21 times the surface.
Strategies for small offices to beat the minimum

items: Coordinate with neighboring tenants in the same strip center or office park to split one mobilization across several storefronts.
Ask your landlord whether common-area maintenance already covers sidewalk washing; many CAM budgets include it twice a year.
Bundle the exterior wash with an interior project such as carpet extraction or VCT scrub-and-recoat so the vendor already has a crew on site.
Request a seasonal plan with two visits a year rather than four, focusing on post-winter salt residue and late-summer gum and spill buildup.
Have your day porter handle weekly sweeping and spot spill response, which stretches the interval between washes.

blocks.text: Strategies for large buildings to drive the rate down

items.name: Publish a measured site map
items.text: Give bidders a marked-up site plan with each zone's square footage, surface type, and drain locations so no one pads for unknowns.

items.name: Separate zones by soil level
items.text: Price main plazas at the routine rate and isolate dumpster pads, loading docks, and smoking areas as per-pad items so heavy soil does not inflate the whole job.

items.name: Commit to an annual schedule
items.text: A 12-month agreement with four fixed visits gives the vendor routing certainty and typically earns a 5%–12% discount.

items.name: Provide water and access
items.text: Free hose bib access and an unlocked dumpster corral reduce tank refills and wait time.

items.name: Allow daytime weekend work
items.text: Avoiding night differentials can save $10–$25 per technician hour.

blocks.text: Volume pricing flattens at roughly 15,000–20,000 sq ft per visit, because beyond that the vendor needs a second rig or a second day. Very large campuses also add wastewater recovery obligations, traffic control near parking lanes, and multiple building entrances that each need edging. Expect the floor to settle around $0.10–$0.12 per sq ft for routine work even on the biggest jobs. Bids far below that should be checked for missing pre-treatment, no drain protection, or an undisclosed cap on hours.
Comparing exterior washing with your interior contract

To budget accurately, put exterior washing on the same monthly basis as your interior janitorial. If a 12,000 sq ft office pays $0.09 per sq ft for interior cleaning three times weekly (13 visits per month at 4.333 weeks per month), the interior contract is about $14,040 per month. A quarterly exterior wash of 3,500 sq ft at $0.24 is $840 per visit, or $280 per month amortized, about 2% of the interior spend.

blocks.title: Small-site warning sign
blocks.text: If a vendor quotes a small entry at $0.15 per sq ft with no minimum, confirm the total in writing. Many will add a trip charge or fuel surcharge on the invoice that brings the visit back up to $175 or more.

faqs.q: At what size does pressure washing stop hitting the minimum charge?
faqs.a: At typical routine rates of $0.20–$0.30 per sq ft and minimums of $175–$350, the break-even sits around 900–1,200 sq ft of surface. Below that, you are paying the minimum regardless of the unit price, so focus on reducing visit frequency or sharing mobilization.

faqs.q: Do large office buildings get volume discounts on pressure washing?
faqs.a: Yes. Buildings with 8,000+ sq ft of exterior surface commonly negotiate $0.12–$0.22 per sq ft, and an annual agreement with fixed visits adds another 5%–12% discount. The savings come from spreading setup costs and running long, uninterrupted surface-cleaner passes.

faqs.q: Should a small suite hire its own pressure washing vendor?
faqs.a: Check your lease first. In multi-tenant buildings, sidewalks and entries are often common area, maintained by the landlord through CAM charges. If you hire your own vendor, make sure the landlord approves, and require a COI naming the landlord and property manager as additional insured.

faqs.q: Why are dumpster pads priced separately even on big jobs?
faqs.a: Dumpster pads carry grease, food waste, and leachate that require hot water, degreaser dwell time, and often wastewater recovery. Pricing them at $75–$175 per pad keeps that heavy soil from inflating the rate on clean plaza concrete, and makes bids easier to compare.

faqs.q: What safety rules apply to pressure washing near building entrances?
faqs.a: Vendors should cone and sign wet areas, keep a clear pedestrian route compliant with ADA accessibility, provide Safety Data Sheets for detergents under OSHA HazCom, and train workers on high-pressure injection hazards. Scheduling before business hours limits slip exposure for staff and visitors.
